title: Campaign: idempotency across the estate
_note: rv2 S2 (PLAN §2.2 campaign-<tag> row, tag idempotency). Ideas say where the guarantee is enforced, what breaks if it moves, and the trade-off the repos chose; sources are 3 live, non-archived campaign study quests from different repos (C# and JS; track js is the section's home). recapAfter = any 3 sources passed. Server-local side file, never stamped.

ideas.idea: An idempotency key is bound to its sender and request: the same key with the same request returns the stored outcome, a different body is refused.
ideas.why: A key that ignores the request lets a client, or a bug, replay one key for a different operation and receive someone else's stored result.
ideas.prompt: A client accidentally reuses yesterday's Idempotency-Key for a new payment with a different amount. What should the server do, and what must it have stored to decide?
ideas.answer: It must not run the new payment, and must not hand back the old result as if it matched. Store the key per caller with a hash of the request (method, path, body) and the outcome; on a hit with a different hash, refuse with a conflict error. Only an identical request gets the stored response.

ideas.idea: A unique constraint written in the same transaction as the effect is what makes a duplicate create safe; a look-first read only speeds up the common case.
ideas.why: Two concurrent requests can both pass a pre-read, and an in-memory key store forgets everything on restart and is not shared between replicas.
ideas.prompt: An idempotency store lives in a process dictionary, and the code checks it before creating a payment. It works in tests. Name two production situations where duplicates still appear, and the fix.
ideas.answer: Two replicas each have their own dictionary, so a retry routed to the other one runs again; and a restart empties it. Two simultaneous requests can also both miss the check. Persist the key in a table that refuses a second row for the same key, written in the transaction that creates the payment, so the second insert fails.

ideas.idea: The caller that retries must keep one key for one logical attempt; minting a fresh key on every click or retry turns idempotency off.
ideas.why: Generating the key per submit means every retry looks like a new operation, so double submits and lost responses create duplicates despite server-side dedupe.
ideas.prompt: The payment endpoint requires an Idempotency-Key, yet a double-clicked form still creates two payments. The form generates a random UUID inside its submit handler. What is wrong, and where should the key come from?
ideas.answer: Each click runs the handler, so each click sends a new random key and the server sees two different operations. Create the key once per checkout attempt (when the form opens or the order is drafted) and reuse it for every submit and retry of that attempt; a new key only for a genuinely new attempt.

ideas.idea: Every side effect a workflow step triggers carries a key derived from the step, unchanged across retries, resumes and replays, so the system that performs it can refuse a repeat.
ideas.why: Replaying failed runs with new keys re-sends charges, emails and webhooks the vendor already performed once.
ideas.prompt: You must replay 10,000 failed workflow runs after an outage. Some steps had already charged cards before the failure. What has to be true of the replay for this to be safe?
ideas.answer: Each replayed step must send the same idempotency key the original attempt sent, for example one derived from run and step, so the payment provider recognises the repeat and returns the first result. Steps that cannot carry such a key need their own record of completion, checked before the effect.

ideas.idea: Delivery is at-least-once, so the consumer dedupes by the event's own id, and marks it done only after the work is complete, not when it starts.
ideas.why: A dedupe record written before the work turns a crash halfway into a permanent gap: every redelivery is then suppressed as a duplicate.
ideas.prompt: A webhook relay records 'event seen' first and then fans the event out to five subscribers. It crashes after two. On redelivery nothing happens. Explain, and fix the order.
ideas.answer: The early record says the event was handled, so the redelivered copy is dropped and three subscribers never receive it. Record completion after the fan-out succeeds (or per subscriber), keep one event id for the event's whole life, and let consumers ignore ids they already completed.
